stimulus.text: On September 9, 1739, about twenty enslaved people gathered near the Stono River in South Carolina, seized guns from a country store, and began marching south toward Florida, where the Spanish offered freedom to enslaved people who reached St. Augustine. Along the way the band grew to about a hundred. A colonial militia caught them, killed many, and executed the rest. South Carolina answered with the Negro Act of 1740, which tightened controls on enslaved people's movement, assembly, and reading, and imposed a prohibitive duty that cut slave imports sharply for about a decade. Most enslaved people did not revolt: with the law behind owners and a white monopoly on weapons, open rebellion was close to suicide, so resistance more often took quieter forms — working slowly, breaking tools, and holding on to African names and practices.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing Barron's 2027 Ch 4, 5 Steps 2024 Ch 8, and Princeton Review Ch 6.

source: original; stimulus is an original secondary passage written for this question
stem: Most enslaved people in the colonies did not launch open revolts. According to the passage, what did resistance more often look like?

options.text: Organized military campaigns against colonial capitals.
options.misconception: Open revolt was rare and close to suicide; most resistance was quieter.

options.text: Petitions to Parliament demanding immediate emancipation.
options.misconception: Enslaved people had no legal standing to petition Parliament, and emancipation was not on offer.

options.text: Quieter acts: working slowly, breaking tools, and keeping African names.
Mass escape to the northern colonies, where slavery was illegal.
options.misconception: Slavery was legal in all thirteen colonies, and escape north was rare and dangerous.

rationales.general:
1. Read what open revolt cost. With the law behind owners and a white monopoly on weapons, rebellion was close to suicide.
2. Ask what resistance looked like instead. Working slowly, breaking tools, and holding on to African names and practices.
3. Ask what those acts did. They slowed the work, cost the owner money, and kept a culture alive — without risking a battle.
4. Name the pattern. Resistance took the form people could afford: daily, quiet, and constant.
Remember: resistance is not only revolt — ask what people did every day to push back.
rationales.C: Open revolt was rare because it was close to suicide: the law stood behind owners, and white authorities held a monopoly on weapons. So resistance more often took quieter forms the passage names — working slowly, breaking tools, and holding on to African names and practices. Those acts slowed the work, cost owners money, and kept a culture alive without risking a battle. The other options are wrong: no military campaigns or Parliament petitions were possible, and slavery was legal in the North too.
rationales.A: Open revolt was rare and close to suicide; most resistance was quieter.
rationales.B: Enslaved people had no legal standing to petition Parliament, and emancipation was not on offer.
rationales.D: Slavery was legal in all thirteen colonies, and escape north was rare and dangerous.
